title: Mastery Challenge: Probability & Statistics
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Probability & Statistics Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: percents, rates, precision, big data, forecasts, algorithms, health headlines and crime counts. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Probability & Statistics Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions from across the tree, from your first percent to the numbers in the news. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Probability & Statistics: mastered
learned: How to read a percent, a rate or a forecast by first asking: out of what?
Why a huge data set or a scary headline still needs the real numbers behind it.
How to judge a forecast or an algorithm by its long record, not by one result.
Which four questions to put to any statistic: of what, compared to what, from whom, how sure.

questions.prompt: A share price starts at $200, falls 50% on Monday and rises 50% on Tuesday. Where does it end up?

options.rationale: That's after Monday's fall only.
The rise is taken from the smaller, fallen price.
Each percent is measured from its own start.

questions.explanation: Down 50% takes $200 to $100; up 50% of $100 adds only $50, so it ends at $150.

questions.prompt: The share of workers who cycle to work rises from 20% to 25%. Which description is right?

options.label: Up 5 percentage points, a 25% rise
Up 5 percent, from 20% to 25%
options.rationale: Comparing two percents gives points: 5 points.

options.label: Up 25 percentage points
options.rationale: Subtract: 25 minus 20 is 5 points.

options.label: Up 20 percentage points
options.rationale: Points are the plain difference, 5.

questions.explanation: 25 minus 20 is 5 percentage points; 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, a 25% rise.

questions.prompt: Village A has 5 cases among 500 people; City B has 500 cases among 100,000. Which has the higher rate per 100,000?

options.label: City B, since it has 100 times the cases
options.rationale: Totals ignore population size.

options.label: They are the same
options.rationale: Work out each rate: 1,000 against 500 per 100,000.

options.label: Village A, twice City B's rate
You can't compare places of different sizes
options.rationale: That's exactly what rates are for.

questions.prompt: A report turns a rounded "about 40 km" into "24.85 miles". What does the story of 98.6°F say about that?

options.label: Miles are more accurate than kilometers
options.rationale: The unit doesn't add accuracy.

options.label: The report must have remeasured the road
options.rationale: Nothing was remeasured; it was converted.

options.label: Round numbers should always be avoided
options.rationale: Round numbers can be honest about precision.

options.label: The conversion added digits, not precision

questions.explanation: Like 37°C becoming 98.6°F, a conversion adds decimals without making the measurement any sharper.

questions.prompt: Why did Google Flu Trends keep guessing too high?

options.label: Some of its matching searches tracked winter, not flu
The CDC kept changing its flu records
options.rationale: The problem was in which searches it trusted.

options.label: Too few people used Google to search
options.rationale: It had enormous amounts of data.

options.label: It ignored searches and used weather data
options.rationale: It used searches; some just tracked the season.

questions.explanation: Terms like high school basketball rose with winter: "part flu detector, part winter detector".

questions.prompt: Tomorrow's forecast says 40% chance of rain. What does that mean?

options.label: Rain will fall over about 40% of the area
options.rationale: That's a common misreading.

options.label: A 40% chance of at least 0.01 inch at your spot
Rain will fall for about 40% of the day
options.rationale: It says nothing about how long it rains.

options.label: You'll get 40% of the usual rainfall
options.rationale: It says whether it rains, not how much.

questions.explanation: It's the chance that at least 0.01 inch of rain falls at a given point during the forecast period.

questions.prompt: Over years, a forecaster's 80% calls came true 80 times in 100. Today one 80% call failed. What do you conclude?

options.label: The forecaster has suddenly become unreliable overnight
options.rationale: One miss is expected: about 20 in 100 should fail.

options.label: An 80% call should never fail if it was made honestly
options.rationale: Only 100% means certain.

options.label: The forecaster looks well calibrated; one miss is expected
The forecaster should switch to saying 100% from now on
options.rationale: That would claim certainty they don't have.

questions.explanation: A calibrated forecaster's 80% calls fail about 20 times in 100. A long record, not one result, is the test.

questions.prompt: Amazon's hiring tool marked down résumés containing the word "women's". What was the root cause?

options.label: Engineers deliberately told it to prefer male applicants
options.rationale: Nobody programmed that; it learned it from data.

options.label: It had far too few résumés to learn anything from
options.rationale: It had 10 years' worth.

options.label: It was only ever tested on the wrong kinds of jobs
options.rationale: The problem was in its training data.

options.label: It learned from 10 years of résumés, mostly from men

questions.explanation: An algorithm learns the patterns in its data, including unfair ones: bias in, bias out.

questions.prompt: Processed meat sits in the same WHO cancer group as tobacco smoking. What does being in that group tell you?

options.label: How sure experts are that it can cause cancer, not how much
That it is exactly as dangerous as smoking
options.rationale: Smoking raises lung cancer risk about 20 times.

options.label: That eating it will cause cancer in most people
options.rationale: About 66 in 1,000 heavy eaters, against 56.

options.label: That it was tested in a single large experiment
options.rationale: The evidence came from many cohort studies.

questions.explanation: The group shows certainty that something can cause cancer, not the size of the risk.

questions.prompt: Police-recorded assaults fall 10% in a year. Using the checklist's "compared to what?", what should you check it against?

options.label: Last month's headlines
options.rationale: Headlines aren't a second count.

options.label: The victim survey, since many crimes go unreported
Nothing: police records count every crime
options.rationale: They count only crimes reported to police.

options.label: The number of police officers
options.rationale: That doesn't count crimes.

questions.explanation: Police data catch only reported crimes. The victim survey asks people directly, so it is the natural comparison.
